name: T-osteotomy genioplasty (mini V-line)
lead: T-osteotomy genioplasty, commonly called the mini V-line operation, is a chin-bone procedure that narrows the chin and, in many descriptions, lengthens it. People seek it to get a slimmer, more tapered lower face with a narrower, more defined chin point. It originated in Korean craniofacial practice. The surgeon makes one horizontal and two vertical bone cuts, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece, and repositions and fixes the remaining chin segment with titanium plates.[3]

It is performed mainly for aesthetic reasons, particularly in patients with a chin described as disproportionately wide. A 2014 report in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery describes narrowing the front of the mandible, including the chin, while leaving the back of the jaw untouched, for patients who do not have an excessive mandible angle.[1] Narrowing genioplasty is described in Korean and Chinese surgical series as part of lower-face contouring, often alongside mandible reduction.[4][5][6] The approach is also discussed as one of several add-on procedures in facial feminization surgery.[2]

Evidence is limited to surgical technique reports and case series by surgeons who perform the operation; no randomized trials were found. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as one option among jaw and chin procedures.

chain: Trapezoid of chin bone removed and segment refixed
Chin becomes narrower and slightly longer
Slimmer, more tapered V-shaped lower face
angle.text: The operation changes the bony width of the chin directly. Patients with a wide chin say the result is a narrower, better-balanced lower face, particularly when the jaw angle is already slim.

paras: In the technique as summarized in an encyclopedic overview, a horizontal cut is made across the chin and two vertical cuts remove a trapezoid-shaped piece of bone. The remaining pieces are brought together and fixed with titanium plates, and the mentalis muscle is carefully reattached. The chin is reported to lengthen by roughly 2-3 mm on average.[3]

A 2014 paper frames the operation as a way to treat a wide chin on its own, without reducing the mandibular angle, so that the lower face looks narrower and more balanced.[1] A 2022 review of 3D sliding genioplasty in facial feminization lists mini V-line, V-line surgery, lateral cortex ostectomy and mandible angle resection as procedures that can complement a genioplasty.[2]

Surgery to narrow the chin is usually combined with mandible reduction, according to the authors of the 2014 report; they propose chin narrowing alone for patients whose chin is wide but whose jaw angle is not.[1]
A standard sliding genioplasty instead cuts a horseshoe-shaped segment and moves it forward or backward.[3] The T-osteotomy differs in that bone is removed so the chin becomes narrower.

Earlier and related Asian series describe narrowing genioplasty combined with mandible reduction: a 2008 report of 39 women used central strip resection to narrow the chin,[4] a 2011 series of 57 patients combined narrowing and sliding genioplasty with outer cortex ostectomy and reported a softer, narrower lower face with improved chin proportion,[5] and a 2014 series of 58 patients described a novel narrowing and lengthening genioplasty followed by mandible border contouring.[6]

Wikipedia notes that men's chins tend to be longer and wider than women's with a more square base, and that chin length can be reduced by shaving bone or by sliding genioplasty.[7] A national survey of 1,417 Chinese respondents found most preferred an oval face with a smoothly tapered jaw angle and a round, pointed chin, and most said they were unwilling to have surgery.[8]

The general risks described for genioplasty include swelling, hematoma, and temporary lip weakness or numbness, with infection, bony changes and nerve damage reported less commonly. Surgeon experience is described as reducing complication rates.[3] The main risks of chin and jaw procedures in facial feminization are described as damage to the mental nerve, tooth root damage, infection, non-union and damage to the mentalis muscle.[7] A 2014 series reported no severe complications during follow-up.[6] Procedure-specific complication rates for the T-osteotomy are not well characterised in published reports.

No randomized or controlled studies were found. Published literature consists of surgical series, including a 2014 technique report on the mini V-line,[1] narrowing genioplasty series of 39, 57 and 58 patients,[4][5][6] and a 2022 review that places mini V-line among the adjunctive procedures in feminizing chin surgery.[2]

timeline.event: A report describes narrowing genioplasty in 39 women to achieve a slimmer lower face.[4]
The mini V-line narrowing genioplasty technique is reported in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery, and a narrowing and lengthening genioplasty is described in a 58-patient series.[1][6]
A review lists mini V-line among procedures complementing sliding genioplasty in facial feminization.[2]

card.summary: Korean chin-bone surgery that narrows and slightly lengthens the chin; supported by surgeon case reports, not trials.
card.note: Evidence is limited to technique reports; carries general jaw-surgery risks such as lip numbness.

quick.overview:
The T-osteotomy, or mini V-line, is a chin operation in which a trapezoid of bone is removed so the chin becomes narrower, and the segment is refixed with plates. It is often discussed for people who feel the chin is wide relative to the jaw angle.

Published evidence consists of surgeon-authored technique papers and reviews; no controlled trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Through the mouth, the surgeon cuts the chin bone horizontally and vertically, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece, and repositions the segment with titanium plates, reattaching the mentalis muscle. Average lengthening of about 2-3 mm is described.
quick.risks: General genioplasty risks include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip numbness or weakness, and less commonly infection, bony changes and nerve damage. It is a surgical procedure performed by oral/maxillofacial or plastic surgeons.
